title: Random numbers, seeds and a result that reproduces

videos.script: Ask NumPy for ten random dice throws. Then ask again, with the same seed. {{dice}} You get the same ten. {{same}} That is not a flaw. A seed is what turns a sample, a shuffle or a simulation into something someone else can check. {{check}} This lesson uses NumPy's Generator, one object that holds its place in a long, fixed sequence. {{generator}} It shows why the older way, one global seed for the whole program, moves your numbers when a library you did not write draws first. {{global}} It draws from the shapes data science uses most: normal, Poisson, exponential, and a choice between categories. {{shapes}} And it finally reads the program that made your data, line by line, as a list of draws in a fixed order. {{program}} Last, what a seed does not promise. Not the same numbers in a future NumPy. And not a true result, if you picked the seed that gave the answer you wanted. {{end}}
